newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Reforms revive Tanzania's key agriculture sector.
newsitem.headline: Reforms revive Tanzania's key agriculture sector.

text.p: Tanzania's mainstay agriculture sector is alive and growing again -- thanks to western-backed economic reforms, a deputy minister said on Wednesday.

Pius Mbawala, deputy agriculture and cooperatives minister, told a gathering of business leaders that the reforms introduced when the country abandoned dogmatic socialist policies in the late 1980s and early 1990s had directly contributed to a rise in producer prices and output.

Reforms in the east African country were launched shortly after founding president Julius Nyerere, a diehard socialist, stepped down in 1985 and paved the way for an International Monetary Fund (IMF) agreement.
Under the reforms, inept and inefficient state marketing boards were dismantled or streamlined and centralised agricultural planning was abandoned.

"Before the policy was adopted, the agricultural sector used to be a burden to the other remaining sectors such as health, education and transport. It used to drain a huge share of our financial resources from our domestic banking sector," he said.

Mbawala said output of cashewnuts rose from 46,000 tonnes before reforms in 1993/94 to 63,000 tonnes in 1994/95. This moved to 81,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and output in the 1996/97 year is forecast at 90,000 tonnes.

Cotton production around Lake Victoria rose from 149,000 tonnes in 1993/94 to 251,000 tonnes in 1995/96, falling slightly to 250,000 tonnes in 1996/97. Tobacco production rose from 22,000 tonnes in 1994/95 to 28,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and 30,000 tonnes in 1996/97, the minister said.
Mbawala said producer prices had also risen in response to the reforms first introduced by Nyerere's successor, Ali Hassan Mwinyi, and continued by current President Benjamin Mkapa.

He said new agricultural products earning good prices for farmers included fruit and vegetables with an earning potential of $2,000 per tonne and the emerging floraculture industry centred on the northern town of Arusha.
Mbawala said some negative features of liberalisation include a deterioration in quality of some crops because of a diminishing role played by the crop boards, now lacking government funding.
Provision of fertilisers to farmers, once a role performed by the state crop boards, had become erratic.

"The divorce of the marketing boards from performing any commercial functions related to their respective crops has rendered the input supply role to remain without any reliable actor to shoulder the supply role," Mbawala said.
He said private commercial operators had now recognised the importance of putting in place schemes to guarantee availability of agricultural inputs.

The Tanzanian Coffee Association (TCA) had designed an inputs credit scheme using a voucher system which would start to operate in the 1997/98 coffee marketing season, said Mbawala. The tobacco sub-sector had also devised a similar scheme for farmers.

Agriculture is the most important sector of Tanzania's economy, contributing more than half of its gross domestic product (GDP) and three quarters of its foreign exchange earnings, principally through coffee exports. Four out of five Tanzanians derive a living from the land.
